title: Authentic Kenyan Terere
community: Luo, Luhya, Kisii, Kalenjin, Kikuyu — enjoyed across many Kenyan communities
author: Mama Akinyi

regionalMap.primaryRegion: Western Kenya, Nyanza, Rift Valley, and Central Kenya
regionalMap.alsoCommonIn: Nationwide — found in homes and markets across all Kenyan communities as an affordable, nutritious green vegetable

heritage.origin: Indigenous to the African highlands — a wild and cultivated leafy green across many Kenyan communities
heritage.history: Terere — amaranth greens — is one of the oldest cultivated and wild-harvested leafy vegetables in Kenya. For generations, families across Western Kenya, Nyanza, the Rift Valley, and Central Kenya have gathered or grown terere in their homestead gardens, preparing it as a simple, quick side dish alongside ugali, stew, or other staples. It is a food of both agricultural tradition and everyday practicality — fast to prepare, deeply nutritious, and available throughout the year.
heritage.modernEvolution: While traditionally gathered wild from roadsides and fields, terere is now widely grown in kitchen gardens and sold in Kenyan markets and supermarkets. Its exceptional nutritional profile has made it increasingly popular in health-conscious communities and urban kitchens across Kenya.

desc: Terere is one of Kenya's most beloved traditional leafy vegetables — fresh amaranth greens quickly sautéed with onions, tomatoes, garlic, and a little fresh coriander until vibrant, tender, and deeply flavourful. Fast, nutritious, and celebrated across many Kenyan communities.
longDesc: Terere — amaranth greens — has fed Kenyan families for generations. Whether gathered wild from the edges of farms and paths or grown deliberately in kitchen gardens, it is a vegetable that requires almost nothing to prepare yet delivers remarkable nutrition. The leaves are slightly more robust than spinach and hold their shape beautifully during cooking. Quick-sautéed with onions and tomatoes, terere becomes something bright, fragrant, and deeply satisfying alongside a bowl of hot ugali.
ingredients: 600g fresh terere (amaranth greens) — washed and roughly chopped
1 cup (240ml) milk — optional, for a creamier dish

substitutions.alternative: Spinach, kale, or Swiss chard — though the flavour is distinctly different

steps: Wash the terere leaves thoroughly under cold running water, removing any damaged leaves, tough stems, or debris.
Roughly chop the leaves and tender stems into manageable pieces. Set aside.
Heat the oil in a large pan over medium heat. Add the onions and cook, stirring, until soft and translucent — about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the diced tomatoes and cook for 4–5 minutes until softened and beginning to break down.
Add the terere leaves to the pan. They will look like a lot — they wilt down significantly.
Stir and toss the leaves with the tomato and onion base. Add 2 tbsp of water to help the wilting process.
Cover and cook for 3–5 minutes until the leaves are completely wilted and tender but still vibrant green. For a creamier dish, stir in the milk at this stage and simmer for 2 more minutes.
Season with salt and black pepper. Taste and adjust.
Scatter with fresh coriander and serve hot alongside ugali, chapati, or rice.
chefTips: Do not overcook — terere should be tender but still vibrant green. Overcooked greens turn dull and lose both colour and nutrients.
A small splash of water helps wilt the leaves quickly without needing extra oil.
For extra richness, stir in a tablespoon of peanut butter or groundnut paste at the end — a popular variation in Western Kenya.
Use the tender stems as well as the leaves — they cook down beautifully and add extra nutrition.
commonMistakes: Overcooking until the leaves turn grey and mushy — they should stay bright green.
Not washing thoroughly — terere can carry soil and grit in its leaves.
Adding too much water — a small splash is enough; too much makes the dish watery.
Discarding the stems — the tender stems are edible and nutritious.

faqs.q: What is the difference between terere and sukuma wiki?
faqs.a: Terere is amaranth, which has softer, more tender leaves and a slightly earthier flavour than sukuma wiki (collard greens). Sukuma wiki has tougher leaves that take longer to cook. Both are beloved Kenyan greens but have distinct textures and flavour profiles.

faqs.q: Where can I find amaranth greens outside Kenya?
faqs.a: Amaranth greens are widely available in African, Asian, and Caribbean grocery stores globally. They may be labelled as callaloo, Chinese spinach, or simply amaranth leaves.

faqs.q: Can I use amaranth seeds as well?
faqs.a: Yes — amaranth seeds are edible and highly nutritious, used in porridge and baking. The GieesK Recipes recipe uses the leaves only, but the whole plant is a remarkable food source.

faqs.q: Is terere the same as spinach?
faqs.a: No — terere (amaranth) and spinach are different plants. They can be used interchangeably in recipes but amaranth has a slightly earthier, more robust flavour and holds up better during cooking.

cookingScience: Amaranth leaves contain oxalic acid, which contributes a very mild astringency. Cooking — even briefly — breaks down much of this acid and makes the nutrients in the leaves more bioavailable. The chlorophyll that gives terere its vibrant green colour degrades rapidly with prolonged heat exposure, which is why keeping cooking time short preserves both colour and nutritional value.
sustainabilityTips: Amaranth is one of the most drought-resistant and fast-growing leafy vegetables in Africa — an exceptionally sustainable food crop.
Terere grows wild in many Kenyan regions and can be harvested from homestead gardens — reducing the need for commercially grown produce.
The seeds can be collected and replanted season after season, making it a self-sustaining crop for small farmers.
storage: Best eaten fresh. Refrigerate leftovers in an airtight container for up to 2 days.
reheating: Reheat gently in a pan over low heat for 1–2 minutes. Avoid microwaving if possible — it makes the leaves mushy.
healthBenefits: Exceptionally rich in calcium — one of the best plant-based sources available.
High in iron and folate — essential for healthy blood and particularly important for pregnant women.
Rich in vitamins A, C, and K — supporting immunity, vision, and bone health.
Very low in calories — just 80 kcal per serving while being highly nutrient-dense.
Contains antioxidants including beta-carotene that protect cells from oxidative stress.
culturalNote: Terere is one of Kenya's most widely shared traditional leafy vegetables — prepared across the Luo, Luhya, Kisii, Kalenjin, and Kikuyu communities among others, making it a rare food that genuinely crosses community boundaries. Whether gathered wild from the edges of farms or grown in kitchen gardens, it has nourished Kenyan families for generations and remains a beloved, affordable daily vegetable in homes throughout the country.
regionalVariations: Plain sautéed terere — just onions, tomatoes, and salt. The classic version.
Terere with groundnuts — peanut butter stirred in at the end for richness.
Terere with omena — dried lake fish added for extra protein.
Terere with milk — a splash of milk added for a creamier dish.
Spiced terere — curry powder or cumin added for extra warmth.
Terere with lentils — protein-boosted vegetarian variation.
